passage: By nine in the evening, Mateo had been at his desk in Valencia since lunch: three past chemistry papers, a history timeline, forty small decisions about what to revise next. When his mother called him for dinner, he said he wasn't hungry and grabbed a bag of crisps and a fizzy drink from the cupboard instead. Then his phone buzzed. Liam had sent a long message about splitting the biology project: who does the poster, who does the talk, which days to meet. Mateo stared at it. His brain felt like wet cardboard. He typed "whatever u want" and threw the phone on the bed. An hour later, Liam replied: "ok, u do the talk then." Mateo groaned. He hated giving talks. On any other evening, he'd have said so.

qa.q: What did Liam's long message ask about?
qa.a: It was about splitting the biology project: who does the poster, who does the talk, and which days to meet.

qa.q: Why did Mateo reply 'whatever u want'?
qa.a: Mateo felt drained and foggy after hours of choosing what to revise, so one more decision felt too heavy and the easiest reply won.

qa.q: What could Mateo do the next time a big choice arrives at the end of a long study day?
qa.a: He could reply that he will answer in the morning, and eat a proper meal before deciding anything.

qa.q: How might Liam read 'whatever u want'?
qa.a: Liam might take it as real agreement, or feel brushed off, not knowing Mateo was simply exhausted.

grounding: Shows a teenager after hours of study grabbing junk snacks and sending a quick careless reply he later regrets.

passage: Exam week at the boarding school meant study hall from four to eight, no talking. When the bell finally rang, Francis stumbled to the mess, skipped the dal and sabzi, and piled his plate with fried papad and gulab jamun. At the table, Lakshmi slid a form across. "Elective choices. The warden wants them by nine." Last week Francis had spent an hour talking about taking Computer Science. Now the boxes swam in front of his eyes. "What did you pick?" "Geography." Francis ticked Geography and handed the form back without reading the rest. Lying in his dorm bed at ten, he sat up with a jolt. Geography? He hadn't wanted Geography at all. First thing in the morning, he went to the warden's office to ask for the form back.

qa.q: By what time did the warden want the elective forms?
qa.a: The warden wanted them by nine.

qa.q: Why did Francis just copy Lakshmi's choice?
qa.a: Francis felt tired and foggy after four hours in study hall, so copying was the easiest option and his own wish slipped away.

qa.q: What did Francis do the next morning, and what could prevent this next time?
qa.a: He went to the warden to ask for the form back; next time he could fill in important forms earlier in the day or ask for time to decide.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel if Francis asks why they picked the same subject?
qa.a: Lakshmi might feel surprised or a bit awkward, having only shared an answer, not meant to decide for Francis.

grounding: Shows a teenager, drained after long study hours, grabbing fried snacks and copying a friend's elective choice.

passage:
Dear Rukmini didi,
You asked how board prep is going, so here's the honest version. The studying is fine. It's the evenings that are the problem. I sit from seven in the morning, and by six I've made about a hundred little decisions: which chapter, which sample paper, redo this sum or move on. After that, I'm useless. Yesterday Amma asked if I wanted rice or rotis, and I snapped, "I don't care, just give me something!" Then I ate a whole packet of namkeen standing in the kitchen and scrolled for an hour instead of eating dinner. Today, the same. I felt awful afterwards, because Amma had made my favourite.
How did you manage this in your boards? Did you have a trick for the evenings?
Your tired little sister,
Jaya

qa.q: What did Jaya eat standing in the kitchen?
qa.a: Jaya ate a whole packet of namkeen.

qa.q: Why did Jaya snap at Amma over rice or rotis?
qa.a: Jaya felt drained and irritable after a hundred study decisions, so even an easy question about dinner felt like too much.

qa.q: What could help Jaya's evenings go better?
qa.a: Planning the next day's study the night before, letting Amma choose dinner without asking, and asking Rukmini didi what worked in her boards.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Jaya snapped and skipped dinner?
qa.a: Amma might have felt hurt, having made Jaya's favourite, and perhaps worried about how tired Jaya is.

grounding: Shows a teenager so worn down by a day of study decisions that evenings bring snapping and junk snacks.

passage: By 8 p.m., Simran had chosen which lecture to skip for the library, which of three canteens to eat at, which elective to drop before the deadline, which project group to join, and what to say to the landlord about the leaking tap in her Kamla Nagar room. When Abhinav texted, "Did you fill the internship form? Closes tomorrow!", she flipped the phone face down. Instead she opened the delivery app and ordered the first thing on the screen, a huge biryani she couldn't finish, and watched episodes until two. At eleven the next morning she remembered the form. Abhinav had already filled his. Hers took twenty minutes, sitting on the stairs outside class, heart pounding, with the portal closing at noon.

qa.q: What did Simran order that evening?
qa.a: Simran ordered a huge biryani she couldn't finish.

qa.q: Why did Simran turn the phone face down when Abhinav texted?
qa.a: Simran felt exhausted and overwhelmed after a day of choices, so the form felt like one decision too many and avoiding it was easiest.

qa.q: What could Simran try on days full of decisions?
qa.a: Put important tasks like the form in the morning, and use simple defaults for evening meals so there is less to decide.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt when the reminder went unanswered?
qa.a: Abhinav may have felt worried or ignored, having tried to help with a reminder.

grounding: Shows a student worn out by a day of small decisions defaulting to impulse and avoidance in the evening.

passage:
"Dolma, are you coming for the movie or not?"
"I don't know."
"Okay. Should I get you dinner from the mess?"
"I don't know."
"Did you decide about going home for Losar? Your mother called me, you're not picking up."
Dolma pulled the blanket over her head. "Pooja, I've decided things all day. Which lab slot, which tutorial, whether to redo the report, which bus to take to the market. I can't decide one more thing."
"So you'll just lie here?"
"Yes. And eat those chips."
Pooja sat on the edge of the bed. "Okay. No decisions. I'll bring rice. The movie's off. And tomorrow at breakfast, you call your mother."
From under the blanket: "Okay. That I can do."

qa.q: Which festival did Dolma's mother ask about?
qa.a: She asked about Dolma going home for Losar.

qa.q: Why did Dolma pull the blanket over her head?
qa.a: Dolma felt drained and overwhelmed after a day of choices, so avoiding everything felt like the only option left.

qa.q: How did Pooja help, and why did it work?
qa.a: Pooja took the small decisions off Dolma's plate and moved the important call to breakfast, when Dolma would be fresh.

qa.q: What might Dolma's mother be feeling after the unanswered calls?
qa.a: Her mother might feel worried or hurt that Dolma isn't picking up, and anxious to know the Losar plans.

grounding: Shows a student worn out by a day of decisions answering 'I don't know' and avoiding everything in the evening.

passage: In my first year at engineering college in Nagpur, I made my worst decisions after nine at night. I'm Hemant, and I only noticed the pattern in the second semester. My days were full of little choices: which assignment first, which lab partner, what to eat, whether to call home. By night I had nothing left. That's when I said yes to things I'd never agree to in daylight, like Ramesh's midnight bike ride to the highway dhaba before a quiz, or buying a game I didn't need. Or I avoided things completely, like emailing my professor about a wrong mark, which I put off for three weeks. Once I saw it, I made a rule: no yes or no after nine. I'd say, "Ask me at breakfast." Ramesh laughed at first. Then he started saying it too.

qa.q: For how long did Hemant put off emailing the professor?
qa.a: Hemant put it off for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Hemant say yes to midnight bike rides that would be refused in daylight?
qa.a: Hemant felt worn out by a day of small choices, so by night impulse won easily and careful thinking felt too tiring.

qa.q: What rule did Hemant make, and why does it work?
qa.a: No yes or no after nine, saying 'Ask me at breakfast', so decisions move to the hours when Hemant's mind is fresh.

qa.q: How did Ramesh react to Hemant's new rule?
qa.a: Ramesh laughed at first, then started using the same line himself.

grounding: Shows a student noticing that after a day of choices, evenings brought impulsive yeses and avoided tasks.

passage: Saurabh, you look like you're about to decide your whole career at nine at night on an empty stomach. Sit, and let old Urmila tell you something. When I was twenty-five and a sub-editor at the paper in Pune, I made terrible choices every evening: the wrong headline, a fight with my editor, once nearly quitting over a comma. My senior, Mrs Karve, watched me for a month and then gave me three rules. Big decisions before eleven in the morning. The same lunch and the same route every day, so small things were already decided. And never decide anything important when you're hungry, rushed or tired. When the Delhi transfer offer came, it arrived at 8 p.m. I wanted to say yes on the spot. Instead I ate dinner, slept, and decided at breakfast. I said no. It was right.

qa.q: At what time did the Delhi transfer offer arrive?
qa.a: It arrived at 8 p.m.

qa.q: What did young Urmila feel when the offer came, and why did waiting matter?
qa.a: Urmila felt a strong urge to say yes on the spot, but knew that tired, hungry evening choices had gone wrong before.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Urmila's story?
qa.a: Following Mrs Karve's rules: eating, sleeping and deciding about the transfer at breakfast instead of that evening.

qa.q: How might Mrs Karve have felt watching young Urmila's evenings?
qa.a: Mrs Karve probably felt concerned and fond, watching for a month before offering rules that would help.

grounding: Shows a young professional saving big decisions for the morning, using routines for small ones and refusing to decide when hungry or tired.

passage: At closing time on the busiest Saturday of the tourist season, the café in Darjeeling looked as if a storm had passed through. Dolma had been on her feet since six: orders, a broken coffee machine, a customer complaint, a missing delivery. Then Siddharth, her business partner, came in waving a contract. "The new milk supplier. They need an answer tonight or the offer's gone." Dolma felt her tired brain lurch towards "fine, sign it". She stopped. She had a rule for this. "No big decisions after a day like today. Tell them seven tomorrow morning." "What if they say no?" "Then it wasn't a good offer." Next morning, after tea and toast, she read the contract properly and spotted a clause doubling the price after three months. She crossed it out and called them. They agreed.

qa.q: What clause did Dolma spot the next morning?
qa.a: A clause doubling the price after three months.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel when Siddharth waved the contract, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: Dolma felt exhausted and tempted to just say 'fine, sign it', but recognised the tiredness and used her rule to wait until morning.

qa.q: Why was Dolma's rule worth keeping even under time pressure?
qa.a: Rested and fed, she read the contract properly and caught a costly clause she would likely have missed that night.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about the delay after the clause was found?
qa.a: Siddharth might have been anxious about losing the deal, then relieved and grateful once the clause was caught.

grounding: Shows a young café owner refusing to make a big choice when worn out and rushed, and deciding well after rest.

passage: Swati used to tease her flatmate Nitin about his 'boring' life in their Andheri flat. The same poha every morning. Five nearly identical blue shirts. The same 8:10 train. Then she noticed something. Nitin, a junior architect, never answered anything important in the evening. When his firm offered him the Pune project at 7 p.m. on a Friday, he said, "I'll reply Monday at ten." When the landlord pressed him to renew the lease over dinner, he said, "Tomorrow morning." "Why?" she finally asked. Nitin shrugged. "By evening I've decided a hundred small things at work. I'm tired and hungry and I say yes to everything. The poha and the shirts mean I don't waste decisions in the morning. The big ones get my best hours." On Monday at ten, he turned down Pune, calmly, with reasons. Swati started laying out her clothes the night before.

qa.q: What does Nitin eat every morning?
qa.a: Nitin eats the same poha every morning.

qa.q: Why does Nitin refuse to answer important things in the evening?
qa.a: Nitin knows he feels tired and hungry by evening and says yes to everything, so he feels safer deciding when his mind is fresh.

qa.q: Which of Nitin's habits did Swati borrow, and why might it help?
qa.a: Laying out clothes the night before, which keeps small morning choices routine so her best hours are free for bigger ones.

qa.q: How has Swati's view of Nitin's 'boring' routine changed?
qa.a: Swati went from teasing it to seeing it as a smart way to save energy, and started copying part of it.

grounding: Shows a young professional using routines for small choices and saving big decisions for his best hours, never when tired or hungry.

passage:
Saturday. For her fifth birthday, Neelam masi took Binita to the huge toy shop in the mall. Aisles and aisles. Binita walked up and down, touching everything, then stood in the middle and burst into tears. Masi carried her out with nothing.
Wednesday. Binita kept asking about the shop, but hid behind Masi's leg when she said they could go back.
The next Sunday. Masi put three toys on the bed at home: a skipping rope, a doll and a puzzle. "One is yours." Binita looked for a minute, chose the puzzle, and hugged it all evening.

qa.q: Which three toys did Masi put on the bed?
qa.a: A skipping rope, a doll and a puzzle.

qa.q: Why did Binita burst into tears in the huge toy shop?
qa.a: Binita felt overwhelmed by aisles and aisles of toys, so choosing just one felt impossible.

qa.q: What did Masi do differently the next Sunday, and why did it work?
qa.a: She offered only three toys at home, a small choice that Binita could manage and feel happy with.

qa.q: How might Neelam masi have felt carrying Binita out with nothing?
qa.a: Masi probably felt disappointed and puzzled, having planned a happy birthday trip, which led her to try a smaller choice.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing and crying among too many toys, then choosing happily from just three.

passage: The Dussehra fair was closing, rain was starting, and Santosh told his son, "Akash, one toy, quickly!" The stall had hundreds: cars, drums, masks, balloons, spinning tops. Akash's eyes darted everywhere. The shopkeeper was pulling down the plastic sheet. "Quick, beta!" Akash grabbed the nearest thing, a tin whistle, and held it tight. All the way home on the scooter he sat silent. At home he threw the whistle on the floor. "I wanted the drum," he sobbed. Santosh sighed and picked it up. Next year, he thought, he'd ask Akash at home to choose between a drum and a car, before they even left.

qa.q: What did Akash grab from the stall?
qa.a: Akash grabbed a tin whistle.

qa.q: Why did Akash throw the whistle on the floor at home?
qa.a: Akash felt disappointed and upset; rushed among hundreds of toys, he had grabbed the nearest one instead of the drum he really wanted.

qa.q: What is Santosh's plan for next year, and why is it better?
qa.a: Asking Akash at home to choose between just a drum and a car, so there are few options and no rush.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt on the scooter ride home?
qa.a: Santosh might have felt tired and a little guilty about rushing Akash at a crowded stall.

grounding: Shows a young child rushed among too many toys grabbing the nearest one and feeling unhappy later.

passage: In the toy shop on Commercial Street, Shankar, four, stood frozen in front of a wall of toy cars. Police jeeps, fire engines, racing cars with doors that opened. He picked one up, put it down, picked up another, then sat on the floor and started to whimper. His big brother Abhinav crouched beside him. "Okay. Just these two," he said, holding up a fire engine and a yellow racing car. "Which one?" Shankar looked from one to the other. Only two. He pointed at the fire engine. On the way home he made siren noises the whole auto ride, grinning.

qa.q: Which two cars did Abhinav hold up?
qa.a: A fire engine and a yellow racing car.

qa.q: Why did Shankar sit on the floor and whimper?
qa.a: Shankar felt overwhelmed by the wall of cars, so picking one felt too hard.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: He narrowed the choice to just two cars, which Shankar could easily compare and choose between.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt hearing the siren noises on the way home?
qa.a: Abhinav probably felt pleased and proud that a simple trick made his little brother so happy.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing in front of too many toy cars and choosing happily once given only two.

passage:
"Forty-two flavours," Gautam read off the board. "I'm getting mango."
Tanvir stared. "Wait. Chocolate chip. No, bubblegum. What's rose-pista?"
"Just pick."
"What's coffee crunch? Is it bitter?"
The man behind the counter tapped his scoop. The queue behind them sighed.
"Fine. Blueberry!" Tanvir said.
They sat on the steps. Gautam licked the mango happily. Tanvir licked the blueberry and frowned.
"I should've got chocolate chip."
"You said blueberry."
"Yeah, but there were so many. Maybe rose-pista is the best one and I'll never know."
"Last week at the cart there were three flavours, and you loved your vanilla."
"That was a good vanilla," Tanvir admitted.

qa.q: How many flavours were on the board?
qa.a: There were forty-two flavours.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir wish a different flavour had been chosen?
qa.a: Tanvir feels unsatisfied and doubtful, because with so many flavours, every one not picked seems like it might have been better.

qa.q: What could Tanvir try next time at a parlour with a long menu?
qa.a: Pick two or three favourites before reaching the counter and choose only from those, like at the cart with three flavours.

qa.q: Why might Gautam enjoy the ice cream more?
qa.a: Gautam decided quickly on mango and didn't keep comparing it with forty other flavours, so it simply tasted good.

grounding: Shows a child taking ages over a long ice-cream menu and then wishing another flavour had been picked.

passage: When our school canteen got a new menu last term, I was so excited. I'm Vishal, and before, there were only four things: samosa, vada pav, idli and poha. Now there were twenty-five: sandwiches, noodles, three kinds of dosa, frankies, milkshakes. On the first day I stood in front of the board so long that the bell rang and I had to grab a cheese sandwich. I didn't even like it. The next day I got noodles and kept looking at Francis's masala dosa. Every day I wondered if I'd picked wrong. Francis just ate dosa every single day and looked happy. After two weeks I decided to copy Francis. Now it's dosa on Monday and a frankie on Thursday. I stopped reading the board.

qa.q: How many items were on the new canteen menu?
qa.a: There were twenty-five items.

qa.q: Why did Vishal keep wondering about picking wrong?
qa.a: Vishal felt unsure and unsatisfied, because with so many choices every meal seemed less certain and someone else's plate always looked better.

qa.q: What did Vishal decide to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: Vishal fixed a simple plan, dosa on Monday and a frankie on Thursday, and stopped reading the board, which ended the daily comparing.

qa.q: Why does Francis seem happier with lunch?
qa.a: Francis picks the same masala dosa every day, so there's nothing to compare or regret.

grounding: Shows a child overwhelmed by a long canteen menu, picking slowly and then wishing another item had been chosen.

passage:
Parent's note after Dhruv's birthday dinner, Sunday. Mahima.
We took Dhruv to the new family restaurant for his ninth birthday. The menu was eight pages long, with pictures. He spent twenty minutes turning pages back and forth, asking what everything tasted like, while the waiter came and went three times. Finally he chose the pasta. When it came, he looked at the next table's pizza and his face fell. "I should have got pizza." Then it was the burger he wanted. He barely ate. On the drive home I realised I had done the same to him with birthday presents: 'Choose anything!' Next time I'll give him two or three options, and let the rest go.

qa.q: How many pages long was the menu?
qa.a: The menu was eight pages long.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv's face fall when he saw the next table's pizza?
qa.a: Dhruv felt disappointed and unsure, because after so many options his pasta seemed less right than whatever he hadn't picked.

qa.q: What does Mahima plan to do next time, and why?
qa.a: Offer Dhruv two or three options, because fewer choices make it easier to pick and to enjoy what he picked.

qa.q: What might the waiter have thought, coming back three times?
qa.a: The waiter might have felt a little impatient, but probably understood a child lost in a long picture menu.

grounding: Shows a child taking ages over a long menu and then wishing he had picked something else, noticed by a parent.

passage: Pankaj, you've had forty college tabs open for a month, haven't you? Your Santosh chacha did the same, just with paper. At nineteen, I had the fat admissions guide, every college in Maharashtra, and I read it like a novel. I made lists, then lists of lists: fees, hostels, placements, the canteen, the colour of the buildings in the photos. I changed my mind every week. Finally the deadline came and I picked the one in Sangli. And for the whole first year, I kept thinking about the others. Maybe Pune had better labs. Maybe Kolhapur had nicer friends. Your chachi, who had looked at just three colleges, loved hers. It took me a year to see that Sangli was good. What stole my happiness wasn't the college. It was the thirty I didn't choose.

qa.q: Which college did young Santosh finally pick?
qa.a: He picked the one in Sangli.

qa.q: Why did young Santosh keep thinking about other colleges during his first year?
qa.a: He felt restless and unsatisfied, because after comparing so many, every college he hadn't chosen seemed like it might have been better.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
qa.a: Seeing, a year later, that Sangli was good and that his unhappiness came from the thirty colleges he didn't choose.

qa.q: How did Chachi's college choice feel different for her?
qa.a: Chachi looked at just three colleges and loved the one she picked, with far less to regret.

grounding: Shows a student comparing dozens of colleges, staying unsure, and feeling less satisfied with the final pick.

passage: Zubin's old phone died two days before his internship started, he had exactly one month's stipend to spend, and the online sale ended at midnight. So he did what he always did: he compared. Thirty-one tabs. Camera scores, battery tests, video reviews, forum arguments. Rajni, sitting on his bed, watched him switch between the same three phones for an hour. "They're all fine, Zubin." "But one of them is the best." At 11:52 he panicked and bought the blue one. It arrived on Tuesday, worked perfectly, and he hated it. Every time he opened it he thought of the grey one's better camera and the black one's longer battery. "If you'd only looked at three," Rajni said, "you'd love this one." He knew she was right, which made it worse.

qa.q: How many tabs did Zubin have open?
qa.a: Zubin had thirty-one tabs open.

qa.q: Why does Zubin hate a phone that works perfectly?
qa.a: Zubin feels dissatisfied and regretful, because after comparing so many, he keeps thinking about the features of the phones he didn't buy.

qa.q: What could Zubin do the next time he has to buy something like this?
qa.a: Set two or three must-haves first, shortlist three options, and pick a good-enough one without reopening the others.

qa.q: How does Rajni see the whole search?
qa.a: Rajni sees that all the phones were fine, and that the endless comparing, not the phone, is making Zubin unhappy.

grounding: Shows a student comparing dozens of phones under time pressure, then feeling unhappy with a perfectly good choice.

passage: In their hostel room in Hyderabad, Siddharth had tried fourteen planner apps in three weeks. Each promised to finally organise his life. He would download one, spend an evening setting up colours and tags, read that another was better, delete it, and start again. His actual assignments sat untouched. "Which one are you on now?" Samir asked from the other bed, writing in a cheap spiral notebook. "The one with the tree that grows. But the one with the calendar view might be better." "You said that about the tree." Siddharth sighed. None of them felt right, because there was always another. Samir held up the notebook. "One. Never looked at another." Siddharth laughed, then stopped. He deleted all the apps but one, and opened his first assignment.

qa.q: What does Samir write in?
qa.a: Samir writes in a cheap spiral notebook.

qa.q: Why does no planner app feel right to Siddharth?
qa.a: Siddharth feels restless and unsatisfied, because with so many options there is always another app that might be better.

qa.q: What did Siddharth finally do, and why was it a good move?
qa.a: He deleted all but one app and opened his first assignment, ending the search so the actual work could start.

qa.q: How does Samir see Siddharth's search?
qa.a: Samir sees it as time lost choosing tools, and shows that one plain notebook, never compared, works fine.

grounding: Shows a student trying app after app, never satisfied because another might be better, until choosing to stop.

passage: Yash, you asked how I found a flat in two weekends when you've been looking for two months. Honestly? I stopped looking for the perfect one. I'm Simran, and in the first week I did it your way: fifty listings, twenty visits planned, spreadsheets. By Friday I was dizzy. So I sat down and wrote three rules before opening a single listing: under thirty minutes to the office, morning light in the bedroom, a lane I'd feel safe walking at night. Everything else was a bonus. Then I only visited places that passed all three, and I stopped at three. The second one had a tiny kitchen, but everything else was right. I took it that day. Do I wonder about the others? A little. But I'm happy. Good enough, it turns out, is really good.

qa.q: What were Simran's three rules for a flat?
qa.a: Under thirty minutes to the office, morning light in the bedroom, and a lane safe to walk at night.

qa.q: How did Simran feel by the Friday of the first week, and what changed?
qa.a: Simran felt dizzy and overwhelmed by fifty listings, then calmer after setting three rules and a limit of three visits.

qa.q: Which part of Simran's method could Yash use right away?
qa.a: Writing a few must-haves before looking, visiting only places that pass them, stopping after three, and taking a good-enough one.

qa.q: How might Yash feel hearing Simran's story after two months of searching?
qa.a: Yash might feel a bit frustrated but also relieved to hear a simpler way that could end the search.

grounding: Shows a young professional setting criteria first, limiting the search to three visits, and choosing a good-enough flat.

passage: I'm Sarika, Sudha's younger sister, and I watched her plan her own wedding food in one afternoon after Mummy had been stuck for a month. Mummy had a folder of twenty-two caterers. Sudha took the folder, sat at the dining table and wrote on the first page: 'Veg. Good dal. Fits our budget. Nobody we've quarrelled with before.' Then she went through the folder and crossed out anything that failed even one line. Seven survived. She rang the first three and booked tastings for Saturday. At the tasting she picked the second one, a small family business with the best dal. Mummy asked, "But what about the others?" Sudha shrugged. "This one's good." I couldn't tell if she was calm inside, but she slept well that night, which is more than Mummy had done in weeks.

qa.q: How many caterers were in Mummy's folder?
qa.a: There were twenty-two caterers in the folder.

qa.q: What do Sudha's shrug and good sleep suggest about how Sudha felt after choosing?
qa.a: They suggest Sudha felt settled and content with a good-enough choice, though Sarika couldn't be sure what was going on inside.

qa.q: Which step in Sudha's approach cut the folder down most, and why does it work?
qa.a: Writing four must-haves first and crossing out any caterer that failed one, because clear criteria shrink a huge list before any comparing begins.

qa.q: How had the month of searching been for Mummy?
qa.a: Mummy had been stuck and sleeping badly, weighed down by twenty-two options with no way to narrow them.

grounding: Shows, through a sister's eyes, a young woman setting criteria first, testing a shortlist of three, and choosing a good-enough caterer.

passage:
Monday. Chetan had forty laptop models open and a headache. His old one had died, and his freelance design work couldn't wait long. He closed the laptop lid with nothing chosen.
Wednesday. Over chai, his friend Kamal made him write three things on a napkin: a good screen for colour work, light enough to carry to clients, within his budget. "Now only three models. No more tabs." Chetan found three that fit and planned a shop visit for the weekend.
The next Saturday. At the store he tried all three, liked the second one's screen best, and bought it in twenty minutes. That night he sent Kamal a photo of his first finished design on it. "Good enough," he wrote, "is actually great."

qa.q: What three things did Chetan write on the napkin?
qa.a: A good screen for colour work, light enough to carry to clients, and within his budget.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel on Monday, and how had that changed by Saturday?

passage: The district kabaddi trials were in Satara on Sunday, and the bus left Wai at six in the morning. Yogesh had practised all summer on the dusty ground behind the temple. On Saturday night, lying awake, he pictured it: the big boys from the city clubs, the coach's clipboard, his name not on the list, the whole village knowing by evening. It seemed safer not to go at all. Then nobody could say he had failed. At six he heard the bus horn and pulled the sheet over his head. Vikas went alone. He didn't get selected either, but the coach told him to come back next year and gave him a training schedule. When Vikas showed him the schedule, Yogesh felt something worse than failing would ever have been.

qa.q: Where were the district kabaddi trials?
qa.a: The trials were in Satara.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh pull the sheet over his head instead of catching the bus?
qa.a: Yogesh felt afraid of not being selected and of the whole village knowing, so not trying seemed safer than a visible failure.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do to be ready for next year's trials?
qa.a: Ask Vikas to share the training schedule, practise with him, and remember that trying and missing still leads somewhere.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel after going alone and not being selected?
qa.a: Vikas might feel disappointed but encouraged, with a coach's invitation and a schedule to work towards.

grounding: Shows a teenager skipping a sports trial to avoid the regret of failing, then feeling the sharper regret of not trying.

passage: All week in Prague, Jana practised the sentence: "Do you want to go to the spring dance with me?" She said it to the mirror, to her cat, to the tram window. Daniel sat two rows ahead in maths, drew rockets on his hands, and laughed at her jokes. But every time she got close, a picture flashed up: him saying no, kindly, and her walking back to her seat while the whole row watched. Better not to ask, she decided. Then nothing could go wrong. On Friday she heard Daniel tell a friend he was going with his cousin's group, because "nobody asked me anyway." Jana looked down at her desk. Nobody asked. She had asked a hundred times, to the mirror.

qa.q: What did Daniel draw on his hands?
qa.a: Daniel drew rockets on his hands.

qa.q: Why did Jana decide not to ask Daniel?
qa.a: Jana felt scared of a kind no and of the whole row watching, so the regret of being turned down seemed worse than never asking.

qa.q: What could Jana try the next time she wants to ask someone something like this?
qa.a: Picture both regrets side by side, including never knowing, and ask privately, away from the whole row, so a no would feel smaller.

qa.q: What would change if Jana had asked?
qa.a: Daniel, who said nobody asked, might well have said yes, or at least Jana would know instead of wondering.

grounding: Shows a teenager avoiding asking someone to a dance, fearing the regret of a no more than the regret of never asking.

passage: In Hingoli, everyone knew what a good son did: pass the bank exam, get a safe desk job. Hemant, twenty-one, had also been offered a place on a year-long wildlife photography course in Pune, the thing he had dreamed about since his first second-hand camera. His sister Preeti found the admission letter in his drawer. "Why haven't you said yes?" "What if I fail? Then everyone says, see, he left a bank job for pictures." "You don't have a bank job." "I'll have one if I take the exam." He took the exam. He passed. At the small celebration, the uncles clapped. That night Preeti found him looking through his old photos of kingfishers by the river, and he didn't say anything for a long time.

qa.q: What course was Hemant offered a place on?
qa.a: A year-long wildlife photography course in Pune.

qa.q: Why didn't Hemant say yes to the course?
qa.a: Hemant felt afraid that if he failed, everyone would blame him for leaving a safe path, so the bank exam felt like the choice no one could criticise.

qa.q: What could Hemant do now to avoid a bigger regret later?
qa.a: He could talk honestly with Preeti and his family about keeping photography alive, perhaps by asking whether the course could be taken later or part-time.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel seeing him with the kingfisher photos?
qa.a: Preeti likely feels sad and protective, sensing her brother gave up a dream to avoid being blamed.

grounding: Shows a young man choosing the safe exam path so no one could call him mistaken, and feeling the quiet regret of not trying.

passage: In Toronto, Jin had two offers on the table: a graduate job at a large insurance company, and a place on the three-person team his friend Nour was building to run community cooking classes for newcomers. Jin loved the cooking classes; he had volunteered at them all through university. But when he pictured telling his parents, and then the project failing within a year, he could already hear it: "We told you." The insurance job came with a lanyard and a certainty no one could argue with. He signed it. A year later, sitting in his cubicle, he scrolled past Nour's photo of a crowded kitchen, a grandmother teaching thirty people to fold dumplings. He zoomed in. Nobody had ever scolded him for his choice. He also hadn't felt like that in a year.

qa.q: What did Nour's team run?
qa.a: Community cooking classes for newcomers.

qa.q: Why did Jin sign the insurance job instead?
qa.a: Jin felt afraid of the project failing and hearing 'We told you', so the safe job felt like protection from blame.

qa.q: What could Jin do now, a year later?
qa.a: Jin could volunteer at Nour's classes on weekends and think honestly about whether the safe path still fits, rather than letting fear decide again.

qa.q: How might Nour see Jin's choice?
qa.a: Nour might understand the pull of safety but miss a teammate who loved the classes.

grounding: Shows a young man picking a safe job so no one could call it a mistake, and later feeling the regret of not trying.

passage: In the college counselling centre, Manoj sat across from Uma ma'am with the stream-change form on the table between them. After his first year of engineering, he could switch to economics, the subject he'd topped in school and still read about at night. "So?" Uma ma'am asked. "If I switch and do badly, everyone will say I wasted a year," Manoj said. "If I stay, at least nobody can say I made a mistake." "And if you stay and spend three years wishing you had switched?" Manoj looked at the form. That kind of regret would have no audience; it would just be his. It felt smaller, somehow. Safer. He slid the form back. "I'll stay." Uma ma'am didn't argue. She said, "The form's here till Friday," and left it on the corner of her desk.

qa.q: Until when would the form stay on Uma ma'am's desk?
qa.a: The form would stay there till Friday.

qa.q: Why does the regret of staying feel 'smaller' to Manoj?
qa.a: Manoj feels afraid of a public mistake, so a private regret that no one else sees feels safer than the risk of being blamed for switching.

qa.q: Why is leaving the form on the desk till Friday a wise move by Uma ma'am?
qa.a: It gives Manoj time to weigh both regrets calmly, without pressure, so fear isn't the only thing deciding.

qa.q: How might Uma ma'am see Manoj's choice?
qa.a: Uma ma'am may see that fear of blame, not real preference, is driving the choice, and hope he will reconsider.

grounding: Shows a student staying in a safe stream so no one can call it a mistake, while inaction carries its own regret.

passage: At the research institute in Bengaluru, Samir had been offered a PhD place in Professor Rao's lab, starting in August. It was what he had wanted for years. But he had also applied to two companies and a fellowship abroad, and what if one of those was the better road? "I just need a bit more time," he told Kunal, the lab manager, in May. And again in June. The companies never replied. The fellowship said no. In the first week of July, Kunal found him in the corridor. "Samir, Professor Rao gave your place to the waitlisted student yesterday. She waited two months." Samir stood very still. He had kept every door open so carefully, and the one he wanted most had quietly closed.

qa.q: When was the PhD place due to start?
qa.a: Samir's PhD place was starting in August.

qa.q: Why did Samir keep asking for more time?
qa.a: Samir was afraid of regretting the road not taken, so committing to the lab felt riskier than keeping every option open.

qa.q: What could Samir have done to avoid losing the place?
qa.a: Set a firm date to decide, compare the options he actually had, and accept the offer he wanted most instead of waiting on long shots.

qa.q: How might Professor Rao have felt during the two months of waiting?
qa.a: Professor Rao might have felt uncertain and a little frustrated, unable to plan the lab while Samir delayed.

grounding: Shows a young researcher delaying a commitment to keep other doors open, until the delay costs him the offer he wanted.

passage:
Dear Minakshi didi,
You asked why I've been quiet. The Pune job is gone. They gave me two weeks to answer and I asked for two more, and then another, because the Bengaluru company hadn't replied and I kept thinking: what if I say yes to Pune and Bengaluru turns out to be the dream? What if I regret it forever?
Bengaluru finally wrote on Monday. No. And Pune had already hired someone else.
The strange thing is, I was never really choosing between two jobs. I was choosing not to choose, because saying yes to one meant saying goodbye to the other, and that felt unbearable. Now I've lost both, and the waiting was the choice after all.
I'll be fine. I'm applying again. But next time I get an offer, I'll give myself a date, and keep it.
Your foolish brother,
Bhupen

qa.q: How long did the Pune company first give Bhupen to answer?
qa.a: The Pune company gave Bhupen two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen keep asking for more time?
qa.a: Bhupen feared regretting the Bengaluru road forever, so saying yes to one job felt like an unbearable goodbye to the other.

qa.q: What does Bhupen plan for next time, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To set a date to decide and keep it, because waiting too long turned into a choice that lost both jobs.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Minakshi would likely feel sad for her brother but relieved that he is talking about it and has a plan.

grounding: Shows a young professional delaying a job decision to avoid regret, until the delay itself costs both options.

passage: Mehak, you asked what happened with my master's plans, so here's the whole embarrassing thing. I'm Farhan. Last year I had admits from Delhi, Hyderabad and a small university in Edinburgh. Three good doors. I couldn't close any of them. Every time I leaned towards one, I pictured myself two years later thinking, you should have gone to the other one. So I asked all three to defer. Then I kept reading about each city, making lists, asking seniors, changing my mind at night. By the time I settled on Hyderabad, the deferral deadline had passed and the seat was gone. Delhi's too. Edinburgh still wanted me, but by then the visa dates didn't work. So here I am, a year later, starting over. The thing I was scared of regretting? I regret the waiting instead.

qa.q: Which three places had given Farhan admits?
qa.a: Delhi, Hyderabad and a small university in Edinburgh.

qa.q: Why couldn't Farhan close any of the three doors?
qa.a: Farhan feared regretting the road not taken, picturing a future self wishing for another city, so every choice felt too risky.

qa.q: What could Farhan do differently this time round?
qa.a: Set a deadline, pick the option that fits best for clear reasons, and accept that a little wondering later is better than losing every option.

qa.q: What might Mehak take away from hearing this?
qa.a: Mehak might feel sympathy for Farhan and see that endless delay can cost more than a wrong choice.

grounding: Shows a young professional keeping every option open for too long, until the delay costs all three admits.
